title: Sustainability
sequence: Introduction (a principle that cuts across the whole project). Later topics apply it to scope, quality, risk, compliance and procurement.

header.html: New emphasis in 2026. Appears in four tasks: Process Task 1 (determine critical information requirements, e.g., sustainability), Process Task 7 (manage cost of quality (CoQ) and sustainability), Business Environment Task 2 (confirm project compliance requirements, e.g., security, health and safety, sustainability, regulatory) and Task 5 (execute a risk management plan, e.g., managing sustainability risks).

Standard §3.7 Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas (3.7.1–3.7.3) · Guide: Scope check results (Table 2-6), Resources §2.6.3, Risk §2.7, sourcing criteria, Appendix X4.8.2 (sustainable contracting), tool "green human resource management"

toc.title: Sustainability Risks, Cost of Quality and Compliance
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1The Principle

Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas: meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own. Consistently integrate sustainability practices across all project areas and all phases; project managers, teams and sponsors are jointly accountable.

  • It means considering people, the planet, society and value while performing project activities, at the tactical, operational and strategic levels.
  • It addresses environmental, social and economic impacts, the well-being of people globally, the wise use of natural resources and sustainable strategies; it may include adopting technology responsibly while identifying and mitigating adverse impacts on the organization, community and environment.
  • Triple bottom line: balancing social equity (people), environmental stewardship (planet) and economic prosperity (profit).
  • Part of the value-driven mindset dimension with Focus on Value (Topic 02).

1.1 The sustainability pyramid

Strategies for any externality a project creates, from most to least desirable:

Rank Strategy
1 (best) Avoid negative outcomes altogether
2 Minimize negative outcomes generated
3 Restore the impacts of negative outcomes
4 (least) Compensate or offset for negative outcomes generated
Exam angle

when choices differ, prefer the one higher on the pyramid (redesign to avoid the harm rather than offset it afterwards).

2Why It Matters: Benefits

Benefit area Examples
Organizational Employee satisfaction and retention, recruitment, better relations with shareholders and stakeholders, optimized risk responses, resilience and organizational learning, better decisions; from resolving ethical dilemmas, stronger governance, legal compliance, lower litigation costs, brand and reputation
Operational Innovation in internal processes, productivity from minimizing waste, designing for sustainability
Financial Cost savings from lower material and energy use, lower operating costs and waste, lower capital expenses, more investment from sustainable finance investors
Customers and stakeholders Satisfaction and innovation from active listening, market growth from demand for sustainable products, stronger reputation, new market opportunities

Sustainability sometimes needs additional funding, but it can reduce financial threat to the project and the funding organization.

3Putting Sustainability Into the Project

  • Requirements and KPIs: sustainability key performance indicators may be written into the scope statement, charter, business case, contracts or other authorizing documents; the sponsor confirms them. Compliance is monitored during planning, execution and closure.
  • Requires: a societal perspective on projects and outcomes; broad stakeholder engagement ("management for stakeholders"); responsible (ethical) leadership; holistic focus on value created and distributed across the broader stakeholder audience.
  • Orientation widens: from compliance-oriented management (focus on the process life cycle, sponsors and team) to achievement-oriented (deliverable life cycle) to sustainability-oriented (outcomes life cycle, all influential community, society, stakeholders and posterity).
  • If sustainability goals are not in the formal documents, the project manager should still encourage discussions about their impact in meetings and with stakeholders (and seek formal confirmation).

3.1 In each performance domain

Domain Sustainability in practice (PMBOK 8)
Governance Transparent, collaborative communication with governance; integrate sustainability goals into governance practices for long-term environmental and social benefits
Scope Embed sustainability in scope so deliverables meet or exceed sustainability goals and environmental and social standards. The WBS or backlog should include activities to manage sustainability, e.g., assess and manage CO2 emissions from project activity or manage the impact on local biodiversity if significant. A scope check outcome: "Sustainability is considered in the project scope"
Schedule Consider environmental impacts; aim to minimize carbon footprint and resource usage; teams can offer ideas to accelerate, slow or stop key activities to maximize opportunities
Finance Include sustainability investments that promote long-term savings and environmental benefit; green benefits may enter requirements; benefits realization through long-term goals
Stakeholders Engagement strategies include sustainability education and collaboration; stakeholders may hold moral rights such as protection of historic sites or environmental sustainability
Resources Prioritize sustainable materials and practices; consider the environmental and social impact of every stage of the value chain (hiring, sourcing, transport, disposal): reduce emissions, use renewable energy, minimize waste, benefit local communities; green human resource management (people policies that support sustainable use of resources and environmental performance)
Risk The team sets the project's risk thresholds; identify and mitigate environmental and social threats; sustainability enables proactive identification of long-term environmental, regulatory and societal risks and creates innovation opportunities
Procurement and sourcing Source-selection criteria may include alignment with organizational values or sustainability goals; sustainable contracting embeds ESG (environmental, social, governance) principles in contracts with measurable outcomes
Quality Sustainability is one of the quality dimensions; embedding quality reduces rework, scrap and waste, which cuts material use, emissions and travel overhead

4Sustainability Risks, Cost of Quality and Compliance

  • Sustainability risks arise when activities fail to balance societal, economic and environmental considerations. Examples: prioritizing cost over environmental stewardship; failing to account for community impacts; underestimating sustainability-related regulatory compliance. Consequences: negative outcomes, stakeholder dissatisfaction, long-term harm to reputation or performance. Record them in the risk register with owners and responses (Topic 21).
  • Cost of quality (ECO enabler): poor quality and rework consume resources and create emissions and waste; prevention and appraisal costs are an investment, while failure costs (rework, scrap, returns) harm both budget and environment (Topic 18). Beyond PMBOK 8 Include sustainability criteria in quality requirements and the definition of done.
  • Compliance (ECO enabler): confirm which sustainability-related requirements apply (environmental regulations, reporting duties, customer or contract clauses), classify them, check threats to compliance, monitor throughout (Topic 23).
  • Challenges: broader scope and time orientation and more stakeholders can raise cost and complexity; there are no universal sustainability criteria so success must be tailored to the project; give the team tools and information to manage sustainability and reduce waste.

5Examples from PMBOK 8

  • Construction: the cheapest materials may harm the environment and health; a sustainability-minded team plans material needs, selects low-impact sources, involves local communities, and considers recycled or natural-process-inspired materials (e.g., urban buildings in wood or with recycled concrete) while still tracking return on investment.
  • Technology projects: eco-friendly practices, lower resource use and waste, improved efficiency; social impact (access to education and healthcare); sustainable materials and minimized carbon footprint.
  • Renewable energy project (risk domain): tailor risk management with regular stakeholder meetings, regular risk assessments and simulation to advance green-energy goals.

[Beyond PMBOK 8] Typical KPI examples (to illustrate; each project defines its own): CO2e emissions, energy and water use, waste diverted from landfill, share of sustainable or recycled materials, biodiversity or community impact measures, supplier ESG compliance rate, workforce well-being indicators.

6Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Goals and KPIs Written into charter, business case, scope baseline and contracts up front Product goals and acceptance criteria; sustainability items in the backlog and definition of done Baseline for committed goals; backlog for evolving ones
Planning WBS activities for sustainability; schedule and budget lines Prioritize sustainability stories by value; re-evaluate each iteration Mix
Monitoring Compliance checks at gates and in reports Review at each iteration; metrics on the radiator Both
Risk Register entries with owners Risk-adjusted backlog includes sustainability risks Both

7Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Sustainability is part of the job, not optional or an add-on. Include it in scope, risk, quality, procurement and compliance.
  2. Missing goals? If sustainability goals are not in the business case, raise them with the sponsor and encourage stakeholder discussion, aiming to confirm them in formal documents. Do not ignore it, and do not invent targets unilaterally.
  3. Prefer higher on the pyramid: avoid, then minimize, then restore, then offset.
  4. Total value, not lowest price. Consider long-term savings, risk reduction, reputation and compliance when sustainable options cost more up front; present the trade-off with data.
  5. Put it in writing: KPIs in the charter, scope statement, contracts, and track them.
  6. Treat sustainability threats as risks with owners and responses; community opposition and regulatory underestimation are classic examples.
  7. Tailor the measures: there are no universal criteria; agree them with stakeholders.
  8. Joint accountability: sponsors, PMs and teams all share responsibility.
  9. Reduce waste through quality: fewer defects and less rework protect both budget and environment.
  10. Procurement: include sustainability criteria and ESG terms when it is an organizational goal.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The business case for a hybrid data-center migration has no sustainability goals, yet the planned hosting site runs mostly on high-emission power and the organization has public ESG commitments. What should the project manager do?

  • ACancel the migration until the organization sets a formal emissions target
  • BSwitch to a greener hosting site quietly and report it at closure
  • CRaise the impact with the sponsor and seek to confirm sustainability goals
  • DProceed with the plan because emissions are outside the approved scope
Show the answer

Answer: C. Sustainability applies across all project areas, so when goals are missing the project manager still raises the impact with the sponsor and seeks formal confirmation. Proceeding blindly, canceling or deciding alone skips that discussion.

S2The evaluation criteria for a freight contract cover only price and delivery time, while the organization has published emissions targets for its supply chain. What should the project manager do before the tender is issued?

  • APropose weighted emissions criteria and agree them with procurement and the sponsor
  • BIssue the tender as drafted and ask the winning bidder about emissions later
  • CAdd a general sustainability statement that carries no weight in the scoring
  • DReplace price and delivery time with emissions as the only scoring criterion
Show the answer

Answer: A. Source selection criteria may include alignment with sustainability goals, so measurable, weighted criteria are agreed with procurement and the sponsor before the tender goes out. Asking afterward, dropping the other criteria or adding unscored wording gives no defensible basis.

S3The business case sets a CO2-reduction target, but the team's backlog contains no items related to it. What should the project manager do?

  • ARemove the target from the business case because no work supports it
  • BReport on emissions only in the closing report of the project
  • CAdd emissions items to the backlog and track the KPI
  • DAssume the contractor will deal with emissions as part of its work
Show the answer

Answer: C. The WBS or backlog should include activities to manage sustainability, such as assessing emissions, so the KPI is planned and tracked. Assuming a contractor will cover it, deleting the target or reporting at the end leaves it unmanaged.

S4A project's rework rate is high. How does this relate to sustainability?

  • ARework is purely a cost and schedule issue with no environmental link
  • BIt does not relate, because sustainability concerns only the finished product
  • CSustainability matters only after delivery, once the product is in use
  • DRework wastes materials and energy, so built-in quality lowers impact
Show the answer

Answer: D. Quality is a dimension of sustainability: fewer defects mean less wasted material, energy and travel as well as lower cost. Treating rework as only a cost issue or as a post-delivery matter misses that link.

S5Residents near a worksite begin protesting noise and dust, and no related risk was registered. What is the best action?

  • ALog it as an issue, engage the residents and plan a response
  • BTell the team to ignore the protests and keep to the schedule
  • CStop work on the site permanently until the residents are satisfied
  • DWait for the protests to die down before taking any further action
Show the answer

Answer: A. The protests are happening now, so they are an issue and a stakeholder concern to be resolved with the community; any related risks are added afterward. Waiting, stopping permanently or ignoring the protests resolves nothing.

S6On a hybrid construction program, a lower-emission option costs 4% more but reduces long-term operating cost and regulatory risk. How should the project manager proceed?

  • AReject the option because it costs more than the baseline plan
  • BPresent a total-value comparison to the sponsor for a decision
  • CPostpone the choice to a future project with a larger budget
  • DAdopt the option immediately and explain the extra cost afterward
Show the answer

Answer: B. Sustainable options may cost more now but save money and reduce risk later, so the project manager presents the total-value comparison and the sponsor decides within governance. Rejecting on price, adopting without approval or postponing avoids that decision.

S7Stakeholders of an agile product ask how sustainability success will be judged, and no standard criteria exist for this type of product. What should the project manager do?

  • ATell the stakeholders that sustainability success cannot be measured
  • BUse whichever measure is cheapest to collect during the project
  • CWait until a regulator publishes criteria before setting any KPIs
  • DAgree measurable sustainability KPIs with stakeholders and document them
Show the answer

Answer: D. There are no universal sustainability criteria, so success is tailored: measurable KPIs are agreed with stakeholders and written into the formal documents. Declaring it unmeasurable, choosing the cheapest measure or waiting leaves no basis for judgment.

S8The contract for a new facility includes an ESG clause that requires an emissions report at handover, but the closing checklist has no such item. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd the report to closure, collect the data and verify compliance before handover
  • BSend a statement that emissions were acceptable without supporting data
  • CAsk the customer to waive the clause informally at the handover meeting
  • DClose the project as planned and let the customer ask for the report later
Show the answer

Answer: A. Compliance with contractual and sustainability requirements is monitored through planning, execution and closure, so the missing checklist item is added and the evidence gathered before handover. Waiting, asserting compliance without data or seeking an informal waiver leaves the obligation unmet.

S9The team can avoid a harmful discharge by redesigning a process, which costs two weeks, or by buying offsets afterward, which is cheaper. Which choice is better aligned with the sustainability principle?

  • ABuy the offsets, because they cost less and protect the schedule
  • BDo nothing until a regulator or resident complains about the discharge
  • CCompensate the community only if residents complain after the discharge
  • DRedesign the process, because avoiding harm outranks offsetting it
Show the answer

Answer: D. The sustainability pyramid ranks avoiding negative outcomes above minimizing, restoring and compensating or offsetting, so redesign is preferred. Offsets are the least desirable response, and waiting for complaints is not a strategy.

S10A global agile program requires frequent international travel for its planning events. Which action best reflects sustainability?

  • AIncrease travel so that the whole team bonds in person at every milestone
  • BHold routine coordination virtually and travel only when it adds value
  • CCancel all coordination meetings so that nobody needs to travel at all
  • DSend the team in larger groups to cut the travel cost per person
Show the answer

Answer: B. Reducing unnecessary travel cuts emissions and overhead while virtual tools keep collaboration effective. Adding travel, canceling meetings or traveling in groups does not reflect the principle.

8.2 Recall Q&As

R1State the sustainability principle.

Show the answer

Integrate sustainability within all project areas: meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

R2What is the triple bottom line?

Show the answer

Social equity (people), environmental stewardship (planet), economic prosperity (profit).

R3Order the sustainability pyramid.

Show the answer

Avoid, minimize, restore, compensate/offset (most to least desirable).

R4Who is accountable for sustainability?

Show the answer

Project managers, project teams and sponsors jointly.

R5Where can sustainability KPIs be recorded?

Show the answer

Scope statement, charter, business case, contracts, or other formal authorizing documents.

R6Give three examples of sustainability risks.

Show the answer

Prioritizing cost over environmental stewardship; ignoring community impacts; underestimating sustainability-related regulatory compliance.

R7When should compliance be monitored?

Show the answer

During planning, execution and closure.

R8What kinds of benefits does sustainability bring?

Show the answer

Organizational, operational, financial, and customer and stakeholder benefits.

R9What is sustainable contracting?

Show the answer

Embedding ESG principles in contracts to promote measurable sustainability outcomes.

R10What is green human resource management?

Show the answer

People policies and practices that focus on sustainable resource use, preserving the environment and improving environmental performance.

R11Give examples of WBS/backlog sustainability activities.

Show the answer

Assess and manage CO2 emissions from project activity; manage impact on local biodiversity.

R12Which ECO tasks mention sustainability?

Show the answer

Process Task 1 (critical information requirements), Process Task 7 (cost of quality and sustainability), Business Environment Task 2 (compliance) and Task 5 (risk).

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Principle Present needs without compromising future generations; all areas and phases
Accountability PMs, teams and sponsors jointly
TBL People, planet, profit
Pyramid Avoid > minimize > restore > compensate/offset
Documents KPIs in charter, scope statement, business case, contracts; sponsor confirms
WBS/backlog Activities such as CO2 assessment, biodiversity impact
Risks Cost over stewardship; community impact; compliance underestimated
Procurement Sourcing criteria on sustainability; ESG in contracts
Resources Sustainable materials, green HRM, value-chain impact
Quality Sustainability is a quality dimension; less rework = less waste
Compliance Confirm, classify, monitor in planning, execution, closure
Challenge More cost/complexity; no universal criteria; tailor
ECO links Process T1, T7; Business Environment T2, T5
First-action pattern Raise it with the sponsor, document goals, compare total value, avoid before offset
